lab_title: AR Heart Anatomy Lab: Chambers, Valves, and Dual-Loop Circulation
top_level_objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart (right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle).
Identify the four heart valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic) and describe their role in unidirectional blood flow.

Trace the dual-loop circulation: deoxygenated blood flow through the right heart to the lungs and oxygenated blood flow through the left heart to the systemic circulation, naming major vessels (SVC, IVC, pulmonary arteries/veins, aorta).
Explain why the left ventricle has greater wall thickness (myocardial mass) and relate this to systemic circulation demands.
Explain how valve mechanics prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle and how this supports efficient circulation.

scenes.brief_purpose: Orient students to the AR heart model, establish spatial context within the thorax, and introduce the four chambers and major vessels.
key_visuals: Augmented 3D heart within a semi-transparent torso
Labeled Right Atrium (RA), Right Ventricle (RV), Left Atrium (LA), Left Ventricle (LV)
Color-coded vessels: superior/inferior vena cava, aorta, pulmonary arteries/veins
student_actions: Observe the model and identify the four chambers; toggle labels on/off; listen to the introductory audio clip (Audio: HeartIntro_Orientation)

scenes.brief_purpose: Differentiate atrial versus ventricular walls and introduce internal features relevant to chamber function.
key_visuals: Cross-section/isometric cutaway showing atrial vs ventricular walls
Color-coded endocardial surfaces; highlight chordae tendineae and papillary muscles in the ventricles
Label highlights for chamber-specific features (e.g., fossa ovalis, trabeculae carneae)
student_actions: Identify atrial vs ventricular walls, compare wall thickness visually, and annotate features such as chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.

scenes.brief_purpose: Present the four valves and demonstrate their opening/closing to illustrate unidirectional flow and cusp coaptation.
key_visuals: Tricuspid valve between RA and RV
Mitral/Bicuspid valve between LA and LV
Pulmonary valve at the RV outflow tract
Aortic valve at the LV outflow tract
Animated cusp movement showing opening and closing
student_actions: Name each valve and describe the direction of blood flow; observe valve motion and coaptation to prevent backflow.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4 — Major Vessels and Blood Entry/Exit
scenes.brief_purpose: Identify the major vessels entering and leaving the heart and link them to chamber connections.
key_visuals: Superior and Inferior Vena Cavae entering the Right Atrium
Pulmonary arteries exiting the Right Ventricle; Pulmonary veins entering the Left Atrium
Aorta exiting the Left Ventricle
Color-coded flow arrows indicating deoxygenated (blue) and oxygenated (red) blood
student_actions: Trace the path of blood from body to heart via the vena cavae into the RA, then to the RV and lungs via the pulmonary arteries; return via the pulmonary veins to the LA and onward to the LV and aorta.

scenes.brief_purpose: Guide students through the complete circulation loop with a color-coded path and pause points at each valve.
key_visuals: Blue path through right heart and lungs (deoxygenated blood)
Red path through left heart and systemic circulation (oxygenated blood)
Pause points at each valve to explain function
student_actions: Follow the blood path in sequence (RA → RV → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → LV → aortic valve → aorta); explain valve function at each pause.

scenes.brief_purpose: Link left ventricular wall thickness to systemic circulation demands and overall pump performance.
key_visuals: Comparative wall thickness gauge overlay (LV thicker, RV thinner)
Scale/metric showing systemic pressure requirements
Text label: 'Left Ventricle: systemic circulation powerhouse'
student_actions: Compare wall thickness visually and numerically; articulate why the LV muscle mass supports systemic circulation and how valves support efficient flow.
